stem: For $0^{\circ}\le\theta\le360^{\circ}$, the graph of $y=a\cos\theta+q$ has its y-intercept at $(0^{\circ}, {=bot})$ and its range is ${=bot}\le y\le{=top}$. Calculate the values of $a$ and $q$. Write your answer as $a=\ldots$ and $q=\ldots$.
solution: The range gives the lowest and highest values of the graph: $y={=bot}$ and $y={=top}$.
The graph of $y=a\cos\theta+q$ is centred on the line $y=q$, halfway between its lowest and highest values: ${=bot}+{=paren(top)}={=bot + top}$, so $q=\frac{{=bot + top}}{2}={=q}$.
At $\theta=0^{\circ}$ we have $\cos\theta=1$, so the y-intercept is $(0^{\circ}, a+q)$. The y-intercept is $(0^{\circ}, {=bot})$, so $a+q={=bot}$.

Check: ${=h}$ is the distance from the middle line $y={=q}$ to each end of the range, so $|a|={=h}$. The value of $a$ is negative because the graph starts at its lowest value, so it is a reflected cosine graph.
notes: Advanced because it uses the objective's own pair of facts, the y-intercept (0 degrees, a + q) and the range, and carries a twist the book's section on the effect of a uses: here a is always negative (the graph starts at its lowest value and is a reflected cosine). The value |a| is half the range, q is the midpoint of the range, and the y-intercept then fixes the sign: a = intercept - q. Unique answer for every instance. q is never 0 so the midpoint step is not trivial; whole numbers throughout (|a| 1 to 5, q -4 to 4, range endpoints within -9..9). The stem deliberately does not call a the 'amplitude' (amplitude is |a|). The sign is always negative on purpose, to keep every instance at the advanced level; a family with a random sign would hand half its instances back to the basic tier. Two blind-solver traps to expect: answering a = +h (missing the reflection) and q = the highest value.
